tips.title: The layers in order
tips.body: **Application → Transport → Internet → Link**. Going down is sending, going up is receiving. Learn them in this order and the protocol questions become lookups.

tips.title: Put the protocol on its layer
tips.body: **Application**: HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, IMAP, FTP. **Transport**: TCP and UDP. **Internet**: IP. The specification assigns them exactly this way, and questions ask directly.

tips.title: HTTPS is HTTP with encryption
tips.body: The **S** is the whole difference: HTTPS provides an **encrypted** version of HTTP, so data intercepted on the way is unreadable. Say **encrypted**, not "more secure", which describes the effect without giving the reason.

tips.title: Ethernet and Wi-Fi are families
tips.body: The specification is explicit that **Ethernet** and **Wi-Fi** are each a **family of related protocols**, not a single protocol. You do not need the individual members. **Wi-Fi is a trademark**; the generic term is **WLAN**.

tips.title: A LAN is small and singly owned
tips.body: A **LAN** covers a **small geographical area** and is usually **owned and managed by one person or organisation**. A **WAN** covers a **wide area** under **collective or distributed** ownership — and the **internet is the biggest WAN**.

why.matters:
A computer on its own is a calculator with a screen. Connected to others it can share files and hardware, be backed up centrally and send a message across the world — and in exchange it can be reached by anyone else who is connected.

The topic is mostly about how that is made to work between machines that were never designed together. The answer is **agreed rules** — protocols — and dividing the job into **layers** so that one part can change without the rest being rewritten. Both ideas are bigger than networking.

examples.title: Why a LAN is not simply a small WAN
examples.body:
Size is half the difference and the half everyone gives. A LAN covers a small geographical area — one site, one building — and a WAN covers a wide one.

The other half is **ownership**. A LAN is usually owned by a single organisation, which owns the cabling and the equipment and can do as it likes with them. A WAN is not: it runs over infrastructure belonging to other people, which is why it is leased, slower and out of your control when it breaks. Both halves, every time: the specification names ownership as well as area.

visual.alt: A table comparing a LAN and a WAN on both halves of the difference: a LAN covers one site and is owned by a single organisation, a WAN is wide and runs over infrastructure belonging to others

examples.title: Why both ends have to agree first
examples.body:
A protocol is a set of **rules for how devices communicate**. Without one, the receiving machine has bits and no idea where the message starts, which part is the address, or what to do when something is missing — the data is not corrupted, it is meaningless.

That is why there are so many of them, each for one job. `IP` addresses and routes. `TCP` makes sure everything arrives, in order. `HTTP` asks for a web page and `HTTPS` is the same thing encrypted — which is the precise answer, rather than "it is more secure".

visual.alt: A table of five protocols and the single job of each: IP addresses and routes packets, TCP guarantees arrival in order, UDP trades that for speed, HTTP requests a web page and HTTPS is the encrypted version

examples.title: Why Wi-Fi arriving did not break the web
examples.body:
The internet's protocols were designed long before Wi-Fi existed, and nothing above the bottom layer had to be rewritten when it arrived. That is what layering buys: each layer deals with one thing and talks only to its neighbours, so the **hardware layer can change completely** while the browser above it carries on.

That is the answer worth giving about layers — not "it makes it simpler", but that one layer can be replaced without touching the others. The four, top down, are Application, Transport, Internet and Link.

visual.alt: A table of the four TCP/IP layers from the top down: Application where browsers and email work, Transport which sets up the conversation, Internet which addresses and routes, and Link which is the hardware and its drivers

steps.title: Networks and their types
steps.body:
**A computer network is two or more computers connected together so they can communicate and share resources.**

**The advantages** of networking machines are sharing **files**, sharing **hardware** such as printers, **communication** between users, **central backup**, and **central management** of software and security.

**The disadvantages** are the **cost** of the equipment, the need for **expertise** to set it up and maintain it, greater exposure to **malware and unauthorised access**, and the fact that if a central part fails, **everyone** is affected.

**The three types the specification names:**

**PAN** — Personal Area Network. Very small, around one person. Only **Bluetooth** needs to be considered.

**LAN** — Local Area Network. Covers a **relatively small geographical area** such as one building or site, and is usually **owned and controlled by a single person or organisation**.

**WAN** — Wide Area Network. Covers a **wide geographical area**, and is usually under **collective or distributed ownership** — no one body owns it all. The **internet is the biggest example of a WAN**.

**The two things that separate a LAN from a WAN** are therefore **geographical size** and **ownership**. Answers that give only size are half right.

rows: relatively small, one site or building
props.title: The internet is the biggest example of a WAN

visuals.alt: A table of the three network types showing the area each covers and who owns it

check.prompt: Which two things distinguish a LAN from a WAN?
options: The geographical area covered and who owns it
The number of computers and the cable used
The speed of the connection and its cost
The operating system and the protocols used
check.solution: A LAN covers a **small area** and is owned by a **single organisation**; a WAN covers a **wide area** under **collective or distributed** ownership. Both halves are needed.

steps.title: Wired, wireless and topologies
steps.body:
**Networks can be wired or wireless**, and the specification asks you to compare them.

**Wireless advantages**: no cabling to install, devices can **move around**, cheaper and quicker to set up, easy to add devices.

**Wireless disadvantages**: generally **slower**, a **shorter range** that walls reduce, more prone to **interference**, and **less secure** — the signal travels beyond the building, so anyone nearby can attempt to receive it.

**Wired networks** use different cables. **Copper** is cheaper and fine over short distances. **Fibre** carries data faster and much further with less signal loss, so it suits **long distances** and **backbone** links — at a higher cost.

**Two LAN topologies** are named, and you may be asked to **draw** them and to **choose** between them.

**Star**: every device has its **own cable** to a central **switch**. With 6 devices that is **6** cables. If one cable fails only **that device** is cut off, and performance holds up well because devices do not compete for one shared line. It costs more in cable, and **if the central switch fails the whole network goes down**.

**Bus**: every device connects to a **single shared backbone** cable. It uses the **least cable** and is cheap, but the devices **share** it, so it slows as traffic rises, and **a break in the backbone brings the whole network down**. Each end of the backbone is closed by a **terminator**, which stops signals bouncing back along the cable. A break leaves two open ends, signals reflect back from them and garble everything else on the cable, so no device can communicate — the network does not carry on as two working halves.

props.caption: Star: six devices, six cables, one central switch

visuals.alt: A star network: six devices, labelled PC 1, PC 2, PC 3, Laptop, Printer and Server, each on its own cable to a switch in the centre

props.caption: Bus: one shared backbone, a terminator at each end

visuals.alt: A bus network: five devices, each on a short drop cable to one shared backbone cable, with a terminator closing each end of the backbone

check.prompt: In a star topology, what happens if one device's cable is cut?
options: The whole network stops working
Only that device loses its connection
The network splits into two halves
All devices slow down but keep working
check.solution: Each device has **its own** cable to the switch, so only **that device** is affected. The whole network stops only if the **central switch** fails. Splitting into two working halves is not how either topology fails: a break in a **bus** backbone stops the whole network.

steps.title: Protocols
steps.body:
**A network protocol is a set of rules for how devices communicate.** Both ends must follow the same rules or the data is meaningless.

**Ethernet** — a **family** of related protocols for **wired** LANs. The specification says you do **not** need the individual protocols within it.

**Wi-Fi** — likewise a **family**, for **wireless** LANs. Two details are examined: **Wi-Fi is a trademark**, and the generic term for networks of this kind is **WLAN**.

**TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol) — sets up the connection and makes delivery **reliable**, splitting data into packets and ensuring they arrive and are reassembled in order.

**UDP** (User Datagram Protocol) — sends packets **without** those guarantees. Faster, with less overhead, but delivery is not assured.

**IP** (Internet Protocol) — **addresses** packets and **routes** them across the network.

**HTTP** — transfers web pages.

**HTTPS** — an **encrypted** version of HTTP, for more secure web transactions.

**FTP** — transfers files between computers.

**SMTP** — **sends** email.

**IMAP** — **retrieves** email from a server, leaving it there so several devices stay in step.

**A memory aid for the email pair**: SMTP **S**ends. IMAP takes **I**n.

rows: a family of protocols for wired LANs
a family of protocols for wireless LANs (WLAN)
reliable delivery: packets arrive and are reassembled in order
faster delivery with no guarantee of arrival
props.title: SMTP Sends; IMAP takes In

visuals.alt: A table of the ten network protocols named in the specification and the purpose of each

check.prompt: What does HTTPS provide that HTTP does not?
options: The ability to transfer files as well as pages
A faster connection to the web server
Encryption, so intercepted data cannot be read
Automatic reassembly of packets in order
check.solution: HTTPS is an **encrypted** version of HTTP. Reassembling packets in order is **TCP**'s job, and transferring files is **FTP**'s.

steps.title: Network security
steps.body:
**Why networks need securing.** The connection that lets computers share files and hardware also lets anyone who reaches the network try to read data as it travels, use resources they have no right to, or plant malware. The specification names **four methods**, and expects you to say what each is, when it would be used, and how they work together.

**Authentication** — proving **who the user is** before letting them in, most often with a **username and password**. Use it wherever access should be limited to known people: logging on to a school network, or reaching a company's files.

**Encryption** — scrambling data with a key so that anyone who intercepts it **cannot read it**; only someone with the right key can turn it back. Use it wherever data could be intercepted: on **wireless** networks, whose signal leaves the building, and for web transactions, which is what **HTTPS** adds to HTTP.

**Firewall** — in the specification's words, *a network security device that monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and decides whether to allow or block specific traffic based on a defined set of security rules*. It usually sits where the network meets the **internet**, and can, for example, block connections from outside that nobody inside asked for while still letting staff browse the web.

**MAC address filtering** — in the specification's words, it *allows devices to access, or be blocked from accessing a network based on their physical address embedded within the device's network adapter*. The network keeps a list of allowed (or banned) **MAC addresses**, so it suits a network where every device is known in advance, such as a small office or a home Wi-Fi. On its own it is weak, because a device's MAC address can be read and copied.

**How they work together.** Each method checks something different: MAC filtering checks the **device**, authentication the **person**, the firewall the **traffic**, and encryption protects the **data** itself if the others are got past. A stolen office laptop has an allowed MAC address, but the thief still needs a login; a visitor who learns a password still cannot join from their own phone. An attacker has to get past every layer, not just one, which is why they are used together.

props.title: Each method checks something different, so they stack

visuals.alt: A table of the four network security methods and what each checks: MAC address filtering checks the device, authentication the person, a firewall the traffic at the internet link, and encryption protects the data, such as Wi-Fi traffic

check.prompt: Which network security method decides whether to allow or block traffic using a defined set of security rules?
options: MAC address filtering
Encryption
A firewall
Authentication
check.solution: A **firewall** monitors incoming and outgoing traffic and allows or blocks it by its **security rules**. MAC address filtering decides by the **device's physical address**, authentication checks **who the user is**, and encryption makes intercepted data unreadable.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Give both halves of the LAN/WAN difference.** **Geographical area** *and* **ownership** — a LAN is usually owned by a **single** organisation, a WAN is under **collective or distributed** ownership. Size alone is a half answer.

**Learn which layer each protocol sits on.** HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, IMAP and FTP are **application**; TCP and UDP are **transport**; IP is **internet**. The specification states this directly and questions ask for it directly.

**Say "encrypted" about HTTPS.** *More secure* names the effect without the mechanism. HTTPS provides an **encrypted** version of HTTP, so anything intercepted in transit **cannot be read**.

**Remember Ethernet and Wi-Fi are families**, not single protocols — and that **Wi-Fi is a trademark** while the generic term is **WLAN**. Both points are stated explicitly in the specification, which usually means they are examined.

**Distinguish TCP from UDP by what is traded.** TCP guarantees packets **arrive and are reassembled in order**, at the cost of extra overhead. UDP drops those guarantees to go **faster**. Neither is simply better: the choice depends on whether a lost packet matters more than a delay.

**Be exact about topology failures.** In a **star**, one broken cable loses **one device**, but the **central switch** is a single point of failure for everything. In a **bus**, a break in the **backbone brings the whole network down**, and heavy traffic slows everyone because the cable is **shared**. Naming *which* failure belongs to *which* topology is what a precise answer does.

**Give a real reason for layering.** Each layer handles **one job**, so a layer can be **changed or replaced without rewriting the others** — which is why moving from a cable to Wi-Fi changes nothing about the web page you are reading. It also makes faults easier to isolate. *It makes it simpler* is not an explanation.

**Say what each security method checks.** MAC address filtering checks the **device**, authentication the **person**, a firewall the **traffic**, and encryption protects the **data**. Saying that shows why they are layered: each one covers a gap another leaves.

**On wireless security, be concrete.** The signal **travels beyond the building**, so anyone within range can attempt to receive it — which is why encryption matters more on wireless than on a cable someone would have to physically reach.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A **network** is computers connected to communicate and share resources.
- Advantages: share files and hardware, communicate, central backup and management.
- Disadvantages: cost, expertise needed, malware spread, central failure affects all.
- **PAN** — around one person; only **Bluetooth** is needed.
- **LAN** — small area, **single** owner.
- **WAN** — wide area, **collective or distributed** ownership; the **internet** is the biggest.
- **Wireless**: mobile and cheap to set up, but slower, shorter range and **less secure**.
- **Fibre** carries data further and faster than **copper**, at greater cost.
- **Star**: one cable per device to a switch; one break loses **one device**; the **switch** is the weak point.
- **Bus**: one shared backbone; least cable; a break in the backbone **stops the whole network**; shared traffic slows it.
- A **protocol** is a set of rules for communication.
- **Ethernet** and **Wi-Fi** are **families**; Wi-Fi is a **trademark**, the generic term is **WLAN**.
- **TCP** guarantees ordered delivery; **UDP** is faster without guarantees; **IP** addresses and routes.
- **HTTPS** is **encrypted** HTTP. **SMTP** sends mail, **IMAP** retrieves it, **FTP** transfers files.
- **Network security**: **authentication** (the person), **encryption** (the data), a **firewall** (the traffic), **MAC address filtering** (the device) — used together.
- The four layers: **Application → Transport → Internet → Link**.

questions.prompt: What happens to a bus network if the backbone cable is broken in the middle?
options: The whole network stops working, not just the part near the break
Only the device nearest the break loses its connection to the rest
The network carries on working at a slightly reduced speed
Traffic is automatically rerouted around the break in the cable

A break leaves two open ends, signals reflect back from them, and **the whole network stops working** — it does not split into two working halves. Losing one device only is a **star** failure.

questions.solution: A **LAN** — a relatively small geographical area, owned and controlled by a **single** organisation.

options: It carries data faster and further with less signal loss
It is cheaper to buy and to install
It is the only cable that works with Ethernet
It does not need to be physically protected
questions.solution: **Fibre** carries data **faster and much further with less signal loss**, which is why it suits long distances and backbone links. It costs **more** than copper, which is why copper is still used over short runs.

questions.prompt: What is a network protocol?
options: The hardware address built into a network card
A physical cable joining two devices
A program that detects network faults
A set of rules for how devices communicate
questions.solution: A protocol is a **set of rules** governing communication. Both devices must follow the same rules, or the data received is meaningless. The built-in hardware address is the **MAC address**.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Wi-Fi does the specification make?
options: It is a single protocol rather than a family
It is a trademark, and the generic term is WLAN
It operates at the internet layer of the model
It is always faster than a wired connection
questions.skill: Wi-Fi as a family and trademark
questions.solution: Wi-Fi is a **family of related protocols** and a **trademark**; the generic term for such networks is **WLAN**. You do not need the individual protocols within the family.

questions.prompt: A video call drops the occasional frame but stays in real time. Which transport protocol is likely in use, and why?
options: IP, because it routes packets across the network
TCP, because it guarantees every packet arrives in order
UDP, because speed matters more than every packet arriving
HTTP, because it transfers data to the application
questions.solution: **UDP** drops the delivery guarantees in exchange for **speed** and less overhead. In a live call a re-sent frame would arrive too late to be useful, so a dropped frame is better than a delay — the opposite of a file transfer, where TCP's guarantees are essential.

markScheme.description: UDP: speed matters more than every packet

questions.prompt: Why is the central switch a weakness in a star topology?
options: Every device connects through it, so all of them are lost if it fails
It slows down as more devices are added to the network
It splits the network into two halves when it fails
It can only handle one device's traffic at a time
questions.solution: A single broken **cable** loses only **one device**, which is the star's strength. But every device reaches the network **through the switch**, so if it fails **nothing** can communicate. Each topology has its own single point of failure — the switch in a star, the backbone in a bus.

questions.prompt: Why is a wireless network generally less secure than a wired one?
options: Wireless signals are slower and therefore easier to read
Wireless data is never encrypted by any protocol at all
Wireless networks cannot use passwords or any authentication
The signal travels beyond the building, so anyone in range can receive it
questions.solution: The signal is **broadcast** and does not stop at the walls, so an attacker needs only to be **within range** rather than to get physical access to a cable. That is why **encryption** matters more on wireless. Wireless can certainly use encryption and authentication — the point is that it must.

markScheme.description: the signal travels beyond the building

questions.prompt: Why is the TCP/IP model divided into layers?
options: It lets four protocols run at exactly the same time
It makes the network run measurably faster overall
Each layer does one job, so it can change on its own
Each layer encrypts the data passed down to it
questions.solution: Each layer handles **one job**, so a layer can be **changed or replaced independently** — which is why switching from a cable to Wi-Fi changes the **link** layer and nothing above it. It also makes faults easier to isolate. Layering does not itself make anything faster.

markScheme.description: one layer can change without the others

questions.prompt: A company must transfer a large file and every byte must arrive intact. Which protocol pair is appropriate?
options: HTTP over UDP, as web protocols suit file transfer
FTP over UDP, as UDP transfers files more quickly
SMTP over TCP, as SMTP is designed for large files
FTP over TCP, as TCP guarantees ordered delivery
questions.solution: **FTP** is the file transfer protocol, and it needs **TCP** underneath because every packet must **arrive and be reassembled in order** — a single missing byte corrupts the file. UDP's speed is worthless here. SMTP **sends email**, not files in general.

questions.prompt: A school wants a new computer room where one faulty cable will not stop everyone working. Which topology, and why?
options: Star, because each device has its own cable to the switch
Bus, because a single backbone is simpler to repair
Bus, because it uses the least cable of the two
Star, because it removes every single point of failure
questions.solution: **Star** — each device has its **own** cable, so one fault loses **one** machine, and performance also holds up better under load. Note it does **not** remove every single point of failure: the **central switch** is still one, so the honest answer names that too.

markScheme.description: star: each device has its own cable

questions.prompt: Describe the four layer TCP/IP model, explaining the function of each layer and naming protocols that operate at each.
questions.solution:
The TCP/IP model divides network communication into **four layers**: **application**, **transport**, **internet** and **link**. Data being sent passes **down** through them, and data being received passes back **up**.

The **application layer** is where the **network applications themselves operate** — web browsers, email programs and similar. The protocols here are the ones a user's software speaks directly: **HTTP** for web pages, **HTTPS** for encrypted web transactions, **SMTP** for sending email, **IMAP** for retrieving it, and **FTP** for transferring files.

The **transport layer** **sets up the communication between the two hosts**, which agree settings such as the **size of packets**. Its two protocols are **TCP** and **UDP**. **TCP** provides **reliable** delivery: data is split into packets, and the protocol ensures they arrive and are reassembled **in the correct order**, re-sending anything lost. **UDP** sends packets **without those guarantees**, which makes it faster and lighter but means delivery is not assured.

The **internet layer** **addresses and packages data for transmission, and routes the packets across the network**. The protocol here is **IP**, which gives every packet its source and destination address so that routers can decide where to send it next.

The **link layer** is where the **network hardware** sits — the network interface card — along with the operating system's **device drivers**. The specification names no protocol at this layer.

**Layering is used because each layer handles one job only.** This means a layer can be **changed or replaced without rewriting the ones above or below it**. Moving a laptop from a wired connection to Wi-Fi changes the **link** layer entirely, and yet the browser, the web page and the TCP connection are all unaffected — they are dealing with their own layer and rely only on the interface to the next one.

It also makes **faults easier to isolate**: a problem can be traced to a particular layer rather than to "the network" as a whole, and each layer can be developed and tested independently.

questions.prompt: A small business is setting up a network in a new office. Discuss whether it should use wired or wireless connections and which topology it should choose, giving a justified recommendation.
questions.solution:
**Wireless** would be quick and cheap to install, since there is **no cabling** to run through a new office, and staff could **move around** freely with laptops and phones. Adding a new device needs no work at all.

Against that, wireless is generally **slower**, has a **shorter range** that walls and floors reduce further, and is more prone to **interference**. The security concern is the significant one: the signal **travels beyond the building**, so an attacker only needs to be **within range** rather than gain physical access to a cable. That makes strong **encryption** and **authentication** essential rather than optional.

**Wired** connections are **faster**, more **reliable**, and more secure, because reaching the data means physically reaching the cable. The costs are the **installation work** and the loss of mobility. Within the wiring, **copper** is cheaper and perfectly adequate over the short runs inside one office, while **fibre** carries data faster and further with less signal loss and would suit a **backbone** link between floors, or the connection out to the internet.

**On topology**, a **bus** network uses a **single shared backbone** and therefore the **least cable**, making it the cheaper option. But the devices **share** that cable, so performance degrades as traffic rises, and a **break anywhere in the backbone brings the whole network down** — a fault that stops the entire office working and can be hard to locate.

A **star** gives every device **its own cable to a central switch**. With six devices that is six cables, so it costs more. In return, a broken cable takes out **only that one device**, and performance holds up much better under load because machines are not competing for one line. Its own weakness is the **central switch**: everything connects through it, so if the switch fails, **nothing** can communicate.

**Recommendation.** I would use a **wired star** network as the backbone of the office, with **Wi-Fi** added for laptops, phones and visitors.

The star is worth its extra cabling cost because a small business cannot afford a single cable fault stopping everyone, and because it scales better as the company grows. Bus topologies save money that is quickly lost to downtime. Wired connections for the fixed desktops give the speed, reliability and security the business needs for its day-to-day work.

Adding **wireless alongside** rather than instead keeps the flexibility staff actually want, without the whole network depending on it. The one weakness this leaves is the **central switch**, so I would recommend keeping a **spare switch** on site — it is a cheap way to turn a day of downtime into an hour.

criteria.text: Compares wired and wireless with advantages and disadvantages.
Compares star and bus topologies for this situation.
Reaches a justified recommendation, acknowledging the trade-offs.

questions.prompt: A school wants only its own students and staff to use its network, each through their own account. Which network security method does this describe?
options: Encryption of every message sent across it
Authentication, such as a username and password
A firewall on the link to the internet
MAC address filtering of each device
questions.solution: **Authentication** checks **who the user is**, usually with a username and password, before letting them on. MAC address filtering checks the **device**, not the person; encryption makes intercepted data unreadable; a firewall filters **traffic** by its rules.

questions.prompt: What does encryption do to protect data sent across a network?
options: It stops unknown devices from joining the network
It checks each user's identity before they log in
It blocks traffic that breaks a set of security rules
It makes intercepted data unreadable without the key
questions.solution: **Encryption** scrambles the data with a key, so anyone who intercepts it **cannot read it**. Stopping unknown devices is **MAC address filtering**, checking identity is **authentication**, and blocking traffic by rules is a **firewall**.

questions.prompt: A company wants to stop computers on the internet opening connections into its network, while staff can still browse the web. Which method fits best?
options: A firewall with rules for the traffic in and out
MAC address filtering on the whole office network
Encrypting every file that is stored on the server
Asking every member of staff for their password
questions.solution: A **firewall** is a network security device that monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and decides whether to allow or block specific traffic based on a defined set of security rules. Its rules can block incoming connections nobody asked for and still allow the web traffic staff start. MAC filtering controls which **devices** join the office network, not what arrives from the internet.

questions.prompt: What does MAC address filtering use to decide whether a device may join a network?
options: The username and password typed in by the user
The rules set for incoming and outgoing traffic
The physical address in its network adapter
The key used to scramble the data being sent
questions.solution: MAC address filtering allows devices to access, or be blocked from accessing a network based on their physical address embedded within the device's network adapter. A username and password is **authentication**, traffic rules are a **firewall**, and a key that scrambles data is **encryption**.

questions.prompt: What is the IMAP protocol used for?
options: Sending email on to a mail server
Retrieving email from a mail server
Transferring web pages to a browser
Transferring files between computers
questions.solution: **IMAP** **retrieves** email from a server, leaving it there so several devices stay in step. **SMTP** sends email, **HTTP** transfers web pages and **FTP** transfers files.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Ethernet does the specification make?
options: It is a single protocol used only on wireless networks
It is a trademark name, and the generic term for it is WLAN
It is the protocol that addresses and routes packets
It is a family of related protocols, not a single protocol
questions.solution: The specification says **Ethernet** is a **family of related protocols rather than a single protocol**, and that you do not need its individual members; it is used on **wired** networks. The trademark with WLAN as the generic term is **Wi-Fi**, and addressing and routing packets is the job of **IP**.

markScheme.description: a family of related protocols, not a single protocol

questions.prompt: A school is cabling the computers in one classroom, each a few metres from the switch. Which cable is the sensible choice, and why?
options: Fibre, because it is the only cable that Ethernet can use
Fibre, because copper cannot carry data inside a building
Copper, because it is cheaper and fine over short distances
Copper, because it carries data further than fibre does
questions.solution: Over a few metres **copper** is **cheaper** and perfectly adequate. **Fibre** carries data faster and much further with less signal loss, which suits long distances and backbone links, but costs more — and copper, not fibre, is the one with the shorter reach.

markScheme.description: copper: cheaper, and fine over short distances

questions.prompt: An office uses MAC address filtering, so only its own laptops can join its Wi-Fi. A thief steals one of those laptops. Which method still stops the thief reaching the office's files?
options: Authentication, since the thief still needs a staff member's login
MAC address filtering, since the laptop's address is still allowed
Encryption of the Wi-Fi traffic, since it stops the laptop joining
A firewall, since it blocks every device inside the building
questions.solution: The stolen laptop's **MAC address is on the allowed list**, so MAC filtering lets it straight in: it checks the **device**, not the person. **Authentication** checks the **person**, so the thief still needs a member of staff's username and password. Encrypting the Wi-Fi protects data from eavesdroppers but does not keep an allowed laptop off, and a firewall filters traffic at the network's edge.

markScheme.description: authentication: it checks the person, not the device

questions.prompt: A network already has a firewall on its internet connection. Why does it still need authentication?
options: A firewall only works on wireless networks, never on wired ones
The firewall checks traffic against rules, not who the user is
Authentication makes the firewall's rules run more quickly
A firewall cannot be switched on until users have logged in
questions.solution: A **firewall** allows or blocks **traffic** according to its rules. Someone who sits down at a computer inside the network, or reaches it through a service the rules allow, sends traffic the firewall lets through. **Authentication** checks **who the user is**, so the two cover different gaps.

markScheme.description: the firewall checks traffic, not the user

questions.prompt: A school links all its computers into one network so that software updates and backups are managed centrally. Which disadvantage comes with that same connection?
options: Every computer stops working if the internet link fails
Each computer now runs its own programs more slowly
Central backup leaves only one copy of each file to lose
Malware on one computer can now spread to the others
questions.solution: Connecting the computers is what makes central updates, central backup and sharing possible — and it is also what lets **malware** on one machine **spread** to the others. The other options are misconceptions: a LAN keeps working inside the school when the **internet** link fails; joining a network does not slow the programs a computer runs itself; and a central backup is an **extra** copy, not the only one. The real disadvantages are malware spreading, the **cost** of equipment, the need for **expertise**, and a central part whose failure affects **everyone**.

markScheme.description: malware can spread across the network

questions.prompt: A dental practice has six computers on a wired network, Wi-Fi for its tablets, and a connection to the internet. Patient records are kept on a server in the practice. Explain how authentication, encryption, a firewall and MAC address filtering could be used together to protect the network.
questions.solution:
**Authentication** checks **who the user is** before letting them in, usually with a **username and password**. At the practice every receptionist, nurse and dentist would have their own login to the computers and the records server, so a stranger who sat down at a machine could not open a patient's record, and each role can be limited to the records it needs.

**Encryption** scrambles data with a key so that anyone who intercepts it **cannot read it**. It matters most on the **Wi-Fi** used by the tablets, because the signal leaves the building and anyone parked outside is within range. The Wi-Fi should be encrypted, and any web system the practice uses should run over **HTTPS**, so patient details crossing the internet are unreadable in transit.

A **firewall** is a network security device that monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and decides whether to allow or block specific traffic based on a defined set of security rules. It belongs on the practice's **connection to the internet**, where it can block connections from outside that nobody inside asked for — so an attacker on the internet cannot reach the records server directly — while still letting staff use the web and email.

**MAC address filtering** allows devices to access, or be blocked from accessing a network based on their physical address embedded within the device's network adapter. The practice knows exactly which six computers and which tablets it owns, so it can list their MAC addresses and refuse anything else — a patient's phone, or a visitor's laptop plugged into a spare socket. On its own it is weak, because a MAC address can be read and copied, which is one reason it is only one layer.

**Together** they check four different things: MAC filtering checks the **device**, authentication the **person**, the firewall the **traffic**, and encryption protects the **data** itself. Each covers a gap the others leave. A stolen practice tablet has an allowed MAC address, but the thief still needs a login. A visitor who learns a password still cannot join from their own phone, because its address is not on the list. And if an attacker does capture wireless traffic, encryption means it cannot be read. An attacker has to get past every layer rather than just one, which is why the practice should use all four rather than choosing the best.

criteria.text: Explains what each of the four methods is.
Applies each method to a sensible place in the practice's network.
Explains how the methods work together, each covering a gap the others leave.

questions.prompt: A web browser fetches a page from a website, and a designer uploads a batch of image files to a server. Which pair of protocols is designed for these two jobs?
options: FTP for the page, HTTP for the files
HTTP for the page, FTP for the files
SMTP for the page, IMAP for the files
IP for the page, TCP for the files
questions.solution: **HTTP** transfers **web pages**, and **FTP** (File Transfer Protocol) transfers **files** between computers. SMTP and IMAP send and retrieve **email**, and IP and TCP address and deliver packets for every application rather than doing either job.

markScheme.description: HTTP for pages, FTP for files

questions.prompt: Which of these is an advantage of connecting computers in a network?
options: Each computer becomes safer from malware
No specialist knowledge is needed to run it
The equipment costs nothing to install
Files can be shared and backed up centrally
questions.solution: A network lets users **share files** and hardware such as printers, and lets files be **backed up centrally**. The others are wrong way round: networks **increase** exposure to malware, need **expertise** to set up and maintain, and the equipment **costs** money.

questions.prompt: An online shop's login page is sent over HTTP rather than HTTPS. What exactly is the risk?
options: The page will load more slowly than it would over HTTPS
Customers' emails are sent without going through SMTP
Passwords cross the network unencrypted, so can be read
Files on the shop can no longer be transferred by FTP
questions.solution: HTTPS is the **encrypted** version of HTTP. Over plain HTTP the username and password travel **unencrypted**, so anyone who intercepts the traffic — on shared Wi-Fi, for example — can **read** them. Saying "it is less secure" names the effect; the mechanism is the missing encryption. Email and file transfer use other protocols and are unaffected.

markScheme.description: passwords travel unencrypted and can be read

examTechnique.body:
Give **both** halves of the LAN/WAN difference — **area** and **ownership**. Know which layer each protocol sits on: **application** for HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, IMAP, FTP; **transport** for TCP and UDP; **internet** for IP.

Say HTTPS is **encrypted** HTTP. Name the right failure for the right topology: a star loses **one device** per broken cable, while a break in a bus backbone stops **the whole network**.
examinerErrors: Separating LAN from WAN by size alone.
Saying HTTPS is "more secure" without saying encrypted.
Treating Ethernet or Wi-Fi as a single protocol.
Using Wi-Fi as the generic term instead of WLAN.
Putting TCP on the internet layer or IP on the transport layer.
Saying a broken cable stops a whole star network.
Claiming UDP is simply worse than TCP.
Explaining layering as "it makes it simpler".
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer gives **area and ownership** for LAN against WAN, and places every protocol on its correct layer without hesitating. It says HTTPS is **encrypted** HTTP rather than "more secure", and knows **Ethernet and Wi-Fi are families**, with **WLAN** as the generic term. It presents **UDP** as a **trade** — speed for guarantees — and picks the right one for a live video call against a file transfer. On topologies it names the **specific** failure of each, including that a star still has the **switch** as a single point of failure, and it explains layering by what it **enables**: a layer can change without the others, which is why moving to Wi-Fi leaves the web page untouched.
